name: Ivan Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for sitting down with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day, and what you did for work before, if you did.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I pray the dawn prayer, make breakfast, and by nine I'm at the kitchen table sending applications and ringing garages. In the afternoon I do an electric-vehicle course online and tinker with an old Corolla I keep at my uncle's yard. Until July I was a technician in the service department at Dalton Motors in Kingsfield, eight years. The dealership was sold to a big group, and they cut the workshop from fourteen technicians to eight, because electric cars need less servicing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it is mostly hype, then good. A bit of automation I can live with, and people still need their cars fixed. But I've seen the electric cars come in and cut the servicing hours, so I know change can bite without any hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a tool, and a tool is only as good as the person using it. I'd tell the lads at the mosque that honest work is never going to vanish. I'd say the government shouldn't be picking winners, and businesses should adapt or fail on their own merits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm not worried about AI taking a spanner out of my hand. I'm worried about the dealership groups cutting workshops and taking apprentices off the books. I did eight years with Dalton, and I'm proud of it, so being on benefits stings in a way I find hard to say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the electric-vehicle course and get the high-voltage safety certificate, then apply to independent garages and fleet depots. I'd go in person with my tool roll and my references. I'd use a diagnostic AI app on my phone now and then to check fault codes, but I'd never trust it without testing the car myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Restless and a bit ashamed. My father ran a shop for thirty years and never took a penny from the state. Taking it myself feels like a stain, even though I know it's only for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your father say about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says work is dignity, and that I should open my own garage if nobody hires me. He's seventy and still thinks it's simple, which I love and which makes me tired. My mother quietly puts a bag of groceries in my car after Friday visits, and I let her, though I don't say so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd trust the diagnostic app only after testing. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because an app guesses from patterns, and a car is a machine with a history. It once told me a misfire was a coil, and it was a vacuum leak. If I'd just followed it, I'd have wasted the customer's money.

say: I'd say AI is a **tool**, and a tool is only as good as the person using it.
I'd say businesses should **adapt or fail** on their own merits.
think: I fear **dealership groups** cutting workshops and apprentices more than I fear AI.
Being on benefits after eight years at Dalton **stings** in a way I find hard to say.
do: Finish the **electric-vehicle** course and get the high-voltage safety certificate.
Visit independent garages and fleet depots **in person** with references.
Use a diagnostic app now and then but **test the car** myself.
feel: Restless and **ashamed**, because my father never took a penny from the state.
S0.quote: A tool is only as good as the person using it.
fieldNote: Pride in his **father's example** makes benefits feel like a stain.
Uses AI diagnostics but **verifies** with his own hands.
Blames dealership groups for the cuts, in line with his free-market, work-first outlook.

steps.text: Finish the electric-vehicle course and sit the high-voltage safety exam
Visit independent garages and fleet depots with my tool roll and references
Use a fault-code app to double-check diagnoses before testing the car
Keep tinkering on the old Corolla at my uncle's yard

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the second one. It's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That reaches the front office first and the workshop later. Booking, ordering parts, checking warranty claims, those were all software jobs already. Hands-on repairs would last longer, but they'd change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to prove their worth by being useful, not by waiting for rescue. I'd tell my younger cousins to learn a trade and learn the software too. I'd say the market will sort it out, but it should be fair, with real apprenticeships, not unpaid internships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think my old workshop is exactly where it bites: a service advisor and a parts clerk were already replaced by software last year. The mechanics are next, because cars are becoming computers on wheels, with diagnostics done remotely. I'd have to be both a spanner man and a screen man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the EV course, then add a diagnostics certificate and try the manufacturer's online training that some garages will pay for. I'd apply to garages doing fleet and van work, since fleets need steady servicing. I'd start asking the AI assistant to explain wiring diagrams, so I learn the language of the new systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, and a bit stubborn. I'm determined, but I'm also aware that determination doesn't pay the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you see in that workshop when the cars changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer oil changes, fewer brake jobs on hybrids, and more waiting for a software update from the manufacturer. The older mechanics like Brian, who is fifty-six, had a hard time with the laptop. He's a magician with an engine but he's lost with the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the garages only wanted people with a degree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to an independent yard that values hands, and I'd offer to work a trial week for free. A man who shows up on time and fixes the thing speaks for himself. Degrees are fine, but they don't turn a bolt.

say: I'd say people prove their worth by being **useful**, not by waiting for rescue.
I'd say the market should be fair, with **real apprenticeships** and not unpaid internships.
think: Cars are becoming **computers on wheels**, so mechanics are next.
I'd have to be both a **spanner man** and a screen man.
do: Finish the EV course and add a **diagnostics** certificate.
Apply to garages doing **fleet and van** work.
Ask an AI assistant to explain **wiring diagrams**.
feel: Uneasy and stubborn, because determination doesn't pay the **rent**.
S1.quote: A man who shows up on time and fixes the thing speaks for himself. Degrees are fine, but they don't turn a bolt.
fieldNote: Believes in **proving himself** at work, a traditional reflex.
Worries for older colleague Brian, who is a **magician with an engine** but lost on a tablet.
Willing to offer a free trial week, which shows how few options he feels he has.

steps.text: Add a diagnostics certificate after the electric-vehicle course
Apply to garages that service fleets and vans
Ask an AI assistant to explain wiring diagrams each evening
Offer an independent yard a free trial week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. I'd say my first reaction is that nobody could prepare in two years, not families, not mosques, not even councils.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say communities have to look after their own, because the state will move too slowly. I'd say the mosque and the families should organise food and rent help. And I'd say jobs should be protected where possible, with a fair notice period.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd think we were facing something like a flood. In two years the thinking work vanishes, and in five the hands-on jobs begin to follow. I'm thirty-four with no savings, and I'd be competing with many men for work that is losing its value. I'd turn to my faith to keep steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mosque and my uncle for a plan to share housing costs and food, and I'd move into my uncle's spare room if the rent became too much. I'd put my EV certificate to use at any garage that will have me, even part-time. I'd also learn a basic trade that stays hands-on, like plumbing, to broaden my chances.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd feel heavy and sick. I'd pray more, and I'd try not to show my parents how afraid I was. It's the kind of fear that sits at the back of your throat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go on a Friday after prayers and say it straight, the way my father taught me: here's the situation, here's my plan. He'd go quiet and then say we'd manage. I'd want him to believe me, even if I don't fully believe it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the three-year gap before robots do hands-on work matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters for plumbing and engines and building. A robot that can lift a gearbox is a long way from one that can find a hidden leak in an old house. So I'd lean into trades where each job is different, and a machine would struggle.

I'd say jobs deserve a fair **notice period**.
think: It would feel like a **flood**, with thinking work going first and hands-on jobs following.
I'd be competing with many men for work that **loses value**.
do: Ask the mosque and my uncle to share **housing and food** costs.
Use my EV certificate at any garage, even **part-time**.
Learn a hands-on trade like **plumbing** to broaden my chances.
feel: Heavy and sick, with a fear that sits at the **back of the throat**.
S2.quote: A robot that can lift a gearbox is a long way from one that can find a hidden leak in an old house.
fieldNote: Uses **faith and family** as the first safety net.
Judges which trades **resist robots** by how different each job is.
Hides fear from his parents, protecting their peace.

steps.text: Ask the mosque and my uncle to share housing and food costs
Start a basic plumbing course at the college
Take part-time garage work using my electric-vehicle certificate
Move into my uncle's spare room if the rent becomes too much

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is better. It's still a quick storm, but I could build something in that time, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to put proper apprenticeships back, if employers are serious. I'd say families should plan, put money by, and teach their children a trade. And I'd say governments should stay out of the way, but make sure the training is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think I could survive five years by being useful: EV and hybrid work, then diagnostics, and a bit of fleet maintenance. When the hands-on robots arrive around 2034, I'd want to be the man who supervises them, or who fixes the ones that break. I'd also like a small workshop of my own by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work in a garage for two or three years, finish my certificates, and save every month towards a lease on a small unit. I'd use AI for paperwork and booking, to keep costs down. I'd also take on one apprentice, because I believe a trade should be passed on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and focused. It feels like preparing for a long drive: you check the oil, the tyres, the route, and you go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes when you compare this with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 I'd just be holding on. With five years I can be building, because I'd have time to work, save and learn. It's the difference between patching a car and restoring one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the workshop need to survive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A few steady customers like taxi drivers and delivery firms, a good reputation, and low rent. I'd keep my books simple, and use an AI tool for invoices so I'm not up at midnight with paperwork. It's an honest business, and I'd never cut corners.

say: I'd say five years is enough to put **proper apprenticeships** back if employers are serious.
I'd say families should **plan, save**, and teach their children a trade.
think: I could survive by being useful: **EV, diagnostics** and fleet maintenance.
By 2034 I'd want to be the man who **supervises or fixes** the robots.
do: Work in a garage two or three years and save toward a small **unit lease**.
Use AI for **paperwork and booking** to keep costs down.
Take on one **apprentice** to pass the trade on.
feel: Hopeful and focused, like preparing for a **long drive**.
S3.quote: With five years I can be building, because I'd have time to work, save and learn. It's the difference between patching a car and restoring one.
fieldNote: Imagines **supervising or repairing** the robots when they arrive.
Wants to **pass the trade on** through an apprentice.
Anxious because the first garage job and the lease savings are still unsecured.

steps.text: Take a garage job and finish the EV and diagnostics certificates
Save monthly towards a lease on a small workshop unit
Use an AI tool for invoices and customer bookings
Buy a diagnostic scanner and a lift for the workshop when affordable

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the fifth is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd say that's long enough to build a proper life, with a workshop, a family, maybe even teaching others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time for every young person to learn a trade, and for the old to be looked after. I'd say we should invest in apprenticeships and families, not in handouts that go nowhere. And I'd say faith and community will matter more, not less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd feel quite steady about ten years. I'd work, save and grow a small business, and probably marry by then and have children to think about. My worry is whether what I build will be sold to a big chain, as happened to Dalton.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a garage job first, then open my own workshop within four years, with an apprentice and maybe a second mechanic. I'd save for my own place, and maybe start a family. I'd also keep training in whatever new systems arrive, so that the workshop stays ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with a steady sort of hope. It's not a carefree calm, because I'm still on benefits today, and I have to get through the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned marrying. How does that fit into the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mother has been dropping hints for years, and I'd like to settle down, but I won't ask anyone to share a struggle. If I'm earning and have a trade in my hands, it's a fair thing to offer. So work first, family next, in that order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take any steady garage job, keep my hours reliable, and put away something every pay day, however small. I'd also learn the paperwork side of running a business from a friend who owns a tyre shop. A year of steady habits can change a man's whole direction.

say: I'd say every young person should learn a **trade**, and the old should be looked after.
I'd say faith and **community** will matter more, not less.
think: I'd feel **steady** about ten years: work, save and grow a small business.
My worry is a small business being **sold to a chain**.

Save for my own place and maybe start a **family**.
Keep training in new **systems** so the workshop stays ahead.
feel: Fairly calm with steady hope, though I'm still on **benefits** today.
S4.quote: A year of steady habits can change a man's whole direction.
fieldNote: Plans family and business in a clear order: **work first**, family next.
Fears being **swallowed by a chain** as Dalton was.
Anxious today but quietly hopeful over the ten years.

steps.text: Take any steady garage job and keep hours reliable
Put away something every pay day, however small
Open my own workshop within four years with an apprentice
Settle down and marry once I'm earning and settled

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. Two years is too short to retrain, save and open anything of my own, and I'm starting with nothing in the bank. What would help is real apprenticeships, a job at the end of the training, and communities like my mosque looking after their own.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me aren't asking for something for nothing. Give a man a trade, a fair chance and a bit of time, and he'll stand on his own feet. I'd like to be that man again.

headlineQuote: Give a man a trade, a fair chance and a bit of time, and he'll stand on his own feet.
portrait: Ivan is **34**, lives alone in Kingsfield, and has been on **benefits only** since Dalton Motors cut its workshop in July.
He was a car technician for eight years, so benefits feel like a **stain** to him.
He uses AI tools sometimes, such as fault-code apps, but always **checks by hand**.
He blames dealership groups, wants real apprenticeships over handouts, and is anxious in most scenarios and **alarmed** at two years.
He dreams of a **small workshop** with an apprentice and, in time, a family.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years is too short to retrain, save or open a workshop.
whatWouldHelp: **Real apprenticeships** with a job at the end of the training.
**Community** support, such as his mosque, looking after its own.
